anchors: check each candidate image's `WinSxS` for folders of exactly those versions offline
decision: Before a RestoreHealth run with an image as /Source, the image is chosen by checking its WinSxS offline for the exact payload versions the CBS log names as corrupt.

evidence.text: 3724 corrupt payloads of one older revision: Windows Update repaired 0, the current release ISO failed 0x800F0915, the previous release ISO repaired 3724 of 3724.

reopen_if: Microsoft ships a repair source that carries every superseded revision.
why: Superseded revisions live only in the media of the release that shipped them, so a newer ISO can miss them and Windows Update may serve none.

anchors: A probe that kills ScanHealth at a timeout has NO verdict
decision: A probe that kills ScanHealth at a timeout reports could not run (timeout), never health unknown or corrupt; ScanHealth duration is measured, not quoted.

evidence.text: A 1800 s timeout refused two healthy bases as health unknown; a hand run of the same scan found no corruption.

reopen_if: DISM gains a bounded-time health check.
why: ScanHealth ran 27 and 44 minutes on nested-virtualisation guests, and a probe reading a timeout as a health verdict refused healthy machines.

anchors: and treat a loss as a finding of the repair
Never take the key from the registry value `SoftwareProtectionPlatform\BackupProductKeyDefault`
decision: Read SoftwareLicensingProduct LicenseStatus and PartialProductKey before setup.exe and after the apply reboot of an in-place repair upgrade; a loss of activation is a finding. Never use BackupProductKeyDefault as the installed key or as the key to re-install.

evidence.text: Queued lessons 2026-11-16: two MAK guests came back LicenseStatus=5 after a repair upgrade, noticed only after re-baking; an activated guest showed an installed key different from BackupProductKeyDefault.

reopen_if: A measurement shows BackupProductKeyDefault always equals the installed key, or a repair upgrade is shown to preserve activation reliably.
why: A repair upgrade can come back unactivated with nothing in its own result saying so, and BackupProductKeyDefault can differ from the installed key, so a before-and-after check of that slot compares a leftover with itself.

anchors: `0x803F7001` on a MAK is not proof the key is bad
decision: Get the activation error from slmgr /ato (or Security-SPP event 8198), not from the CIM Activate method; treat 0x803F7001 on a MAK as possibly transient and retry later before swapping keys.

evidence.text: Queued lessons 2026-11-16: CIM Activate gave -2146233088 only; the same key failed /ato with 0x803F7001 at two times ten minutes apart and showed LicenseStatus=1 after a later boot.

reopen_if: 0x803F7001 on a MAK is shown to be a permanent key fault, or the CIM method is shown to return the real HRESULT.
why: The CIM method surfaces only a generic 0x80131500, and a key that failed /ato with 0x803F7001 twice was activated after a later boot, so a key swap on the first failure spends a MAK activation on a key that was fine.

decision: Do not state that the BackupProductKeyDefault key is invalid, that it caused the post-repair 0x803F7001, or that the remedy is to swap it for another key.

evidence.text: Queued correction 2026-11-16: the key blamed at two failed /ato runs was Licensed about 35 minutes later.

reopen_if: A controlled run shows a repair upgrade installing a backup-slot key that never activates while the original key does.
why: Refuted by measurement: the same key that failed /ato with 0x803F7001 later showed LicenseStatus=1 on a later boot. Only the measured part (the backup slot can differ from the installed key) is in the text.

anchors: A script that captures its output must mask the key before printing or saving anything
decision: A script capturing slmgr /ipk output masks the product key, case-insensitively, before printing or saving it.

evidence.text: Queued lesson 2026-11-16 (inherited): an /ipk line was saved unmasked to a scratch file. Measured here in pwsh on a fake key-shaped string: -replace [regex]::Escape($key) masked an upper-case print of a lower-case key; String.Replace left it in.

reopen_if: slmgr stops echoing the key in its /ipk success message.
why: slmgr /ipk prints the full key in its success line, and String.Replace misses it when the variable's case differs from slmgr's upper-case print, so a log or scratch file ends up holding a customer key.

anchors: on its own line after the DISM call
decision: Record DISM's exit code in a .cmd with the redirect first (>file echo RC=%ERRORLEVEL%) on its own line.

evidence.text: Queued lesson 2026-11-16: measured on a Windows VM, exit 2 left rc.txt empty and a fleet driver waited its 4 h ceiling.

reopen_if: Never, unless the recording moves out of cmd entirely.
why: echo RC=%ERRORLEVEL%> file expands to RC=2> for exit 2, cmd reads 2> as a stderr redirect and the file is empty, so a driver polling for RC= waits out its ceiling.

anchors: Read the TARGET state on every such line before reporting what a KB did
Before calling a KB the pending cumulative update, read its package identity
decision: Read the target state on a Setup-log package line (Staged is not Installed) and the KB's package identity in CBS.log before reporting it as the pending cumulative update.

evidence.text: Queued lessons 2026-11-16 on a 25H2 guest: SSU Staged then Installed six hours later; CBS Identifier line named Package_for_ServicingStack.

reopen_if: The Setup log stops reporting Staged transitions, or names the package type on the line.
why: A servicing stack update logged Staged hours before Installed, and the Staged KB was the servicing stack update, not the cumulative update; both misreadings were reported to a user and had to be corrected.

anchors: Size a driver's ceiling from the SLOWEST guest class it will meet
decision: Size a DISM /Add-Package ceiling from the slowest guest class, and on a ceiling read the exit code file and UBR before calling the install failed.

evidence.text: Queued lesson 2026-11-16: 4.7 GB .msu, 47 min vs 2 h 11 min; driver verdict NOT FIXED while DISM wrote rc 3010 later.

reopen_if: Add-Package durations are shown not to depend on the guest's VBS/HVCI class.
why: The same cumulative update took 47 min on a plain guest and 2 h 11 min on a VBS+HVCI one; a 2 h ceiling declared the slow guest not fixed while DISM later wrote 3010.

anchors: Time a reboot wait out from the last `TiWorker` CPU
**the restart is HELD** while TiWorker finishes a staged package
decision: Time a reboot wait out from the last TiWorker CPU progress, never from the shutdown /r request; a guest still up long after the request with TiWorker busy and RebootPending set is a held restart, not a hang.

evidence.text: Measured 2026-11-17 on a Win11 25H2 QEMU base: .NET CU Staged 17:13, shutdown /r at 18:06:02 (event 1074), guest still up at 18:17 with TiWorker on a full core and CBS RebootPending=True (contrib queue entry, inherited).

reopen_if: Windows starts restarting promptly after shutdown /r while a staged package is pending.
why: A fixed 600 s wait for ssh to drop called a working guest dead and stopped a 17-guest update sweep, while Windows held the restart for TiWorker.

anchors: `Stop-Service` and `Start-Service` wait with NO time limit
The 120 s bound is not a verdict on the service
decision: A servicing script bounds every service stop and start with WaitForStatus and a timeout, logs each phase to a file on the guest, skips the delete when a stop timed out, and starts the services again either way.

evidence.text: Measured 2026-11-16 on a Win11 25H2 VBS guest (contrib queue entry, inherited). The PowerShell snippet was not executed here (no Windows host in this session).

reopen_if: Stop-Service and Start-Service gain a built-in timeout.
why: Stop-Service/Start-Service wait without limit; BITS sat in StartPending for 20.5 min after a CU and a cleanup run timed out at 30 min with no output, so finding the phase took a second instrumented run.

anchors: Size every ceiling per guest class, the restart included
a second package of the update
decision: Size install and reboot-wait ceilings from the slowest guest class (a .NET CU on VBS+HVCI: 3 h 45 to 3 h 53 install plus about 1.5 h held restart), and read each round's result code before calling a re-offered KB a failed first install.

evidence.text: Measured 2026-11-17/18 on two openvmm VBS+HVCI bases: round 1 ~19:01 to 22:46 and 22:54, CBS items 716 at 21:00 to 1090 at 22:32; both installs rc=2 (contrib queue entry, inherited).

reopen_if: A .NET cumulative update on a VBS+HVCI guest installs within 2 h.
why: A 2 h ceiling would have failed both VBS+HVCI guests; a re-offered KB after the reboot reads as a failed install when both rounds succeeded.
